title: At the Limits of Computability: Steps Towards Autonomous AI Discovery on the Busy Beaver Frontier
authors: Marco Dos Santos, Vivek Veeriah, Alex Havrilla, Andrew Bolt, Goran Zuzic, Satinder Singh
abstract: Recent breakthroughs in AI for mathematics---ranging from Olympiad medal performances to resolving long-standing open conjectures---have rapidly expanded what automated systems can achieve. Yet these successes primarily concern predefined, human-formulated problems, leaving open how AI systems can autonomously uncover mathematical structure and formulate new questions. To push beyond static challenges, we explore the Busy Beaver (BB) domain, an uncomputable frontier that is fundamentally open-ended. Because no algorithm can compute the Busy Beaver number $\mathrm{BB}(n)$ for every $n$, this domain provides a natural setting for sustained exploration through mathematical conjecture and proof. In this paper, we introduce a Gemini-based agentic pipeline that automatically discovers accelerations of Turing machines, expressed as compact mathematical rules summarizing many execution steps. Our system integrates pattern recognition, automated conjecturing, informal mathematical reasoning, and formal theorem proving in Lean. With this framework, our system autonomously discovered and formally verified novel Collatz-like accelerations for eleven machines in $\mathrm{BB}(6)$. Subject to community acceptance, we provisionally classify these machines as Cryptids, namely machines whose blank-tape executions admit exact, compact mathematical descriptions but whose halting behavior remains unresolved. These results advance the analysis of $\mathrm{BB}(6)$ holdouts on the Busy Beaver frontier and demonstrate the potential of autonomous AI systems for open-ended mathematical discovery in fundamental computer science.

infographic.key_insight: A Gemini-based agent autonomously discovered and formally verified compact, Collatz-like execution rules for eleven six-state Busy Beaver machines whose halting behavior remains unresolved.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The work illustrates how AI-generated conjectures can be paired with Lean verification to produce checked mathematical results in open-ended computational research.
method: Recognize patterns in Turing machine executions.
Conjecture compact acceleration rules summarizing many execution steps.
Combine informal mathematical reasoning with formal theorem proving in Lean.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports novel, formally verified accelerations for eleven BB(6) machines, provisionally classified as Cryptids pending community acceptance.
infographic.watch_item: Verified acceleration rules do not resolve these machines’ halting behavior or overcome the general uncomputability of Busy Beaver numbers.
infographic.paper_title: At the Limits of Computability: Steps Towards Autonomous AI Discovery on the Busy Beaver Frontier

title: On the possibilities and limitations of LLM-based multi-agent systems for multi-criteria decision-making in healthcare operations management
authors: Marco Boresta, Tommaso Giovannelli, Sepehr Namirad, Giulia Riccardi
abstract: Multi-criteria models for healthcare operations need weights that express how stakeholders trade off patient waiting time, provider workload, and operating cost, but these weights are difficult to quantify. Teams of large language model (LLM) agents, each prompted to represent a stakeholder, have been used to supply them. We propose a framework for assessing the reliability of LLM-generated preferences as inputs to multi-objective optimization and quantifying how their uncertainty affects decisions. We study explicit preferences by asking agents to rate the importance of the criteria in an outpatient appointment scheduling problem, and implicit preferences by inferring trade-offs from the agents' pairwise choices between emergency department configurations. The computational experiments show that the explicit preferences respond to the clinic's operating conditions and differ across roles, but deliberation among the agents can erase these differences, whereas simple averaging preserves them. The pairwise choices used to reveal the agents' implicit preferences depend largely on which option is presented first, and we find limited evidence that a statistical model using contextual information alongside presentation order predicts the agents' choices on new comparison pairs better than a model using presentation order alone. We then formulate robust weighted-sum optimization models to account for preference uncertainty. In most cases, these models select different schedules or configurations from those obtained using average preference weights. These results indicate that LLM-generated preferences need an audit of this kind before they are used as optimization weights in healthcare decision support.

infographic.key_insight: LLM-generated stakeholder preferences can inform healthcare optimization, but deliberation and presentation-order bias can distort the weights and resulting decisions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Healthcare decision-support systems should audit agent-generated weights and account for preference uncertainty rather than rely solely on average weights.
method: Elicit explicit criterion ratings for outpatient scheduling from stakeholder-role agents.
Infer implicit trade-offs from pairwise choices between emergency department configurations.
Audit preference reliability and use robust weighted-sum optimization to account for uncertainty.
infographic.evidence_signal: Computational experiments found role- and condition-sensitive ratings, strong presentation-order effects in pairwise choices, and robust solutions that differed from average-weight solutions in most cases.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish that simulated stakeholder preferences reflect real stakeholders; contextual models showed limited predictive improvement over presentation order alone.
infographic.paper_title: On the possibilities and limitations of LLM-based multi-agent systems for multi-criteria decision-making in healthcare operations management

title: Recursive Gradient Retraction Methods for Stochastic Nonconvex Optimization on Stiefel Manifolds
authors: Zhijie Yuan, Lei Sun, Ganzhao Yuan
abstract: Nonconvex optimization on Stiefel manifolds underlies many problems in machine learning and deep learning. However, existing stochastic Riemannian retraction methods often rely on stepsizes that require prior knowledge of the gradient Lipschitz constant, a prescribed iteration horizon, or restrictive batch-size choices. We develop {\sf RGR}, a recursive gradient retraction method for stochastic nonconvex optimization on Stiefel manifolds. Instead of recursively updating gradient estimators in changing tangent spaces, {\sf RGR} constructs them in the Euclidean space and subsequently maps them to tangent space, thereby avoiding vector transport. The method comprises three variants: {\sf RGR-SPIDER} for finite-sum optimization and {\sf RGR-SRM} and {\sf RGR-EMA} for online stochastic optimization. {\sf RGR-SPIDER} is Lipschitz-free and horizon-free, as its adaptive stepsize requires neither prior knowledge of the gradient Lipschitz constant nor a prescribed iteration horizon. {\sf RGR-SRM} and {\sf RGR-EMA} are mini-batch and horizon-free methods whose convergence guarantees do not rely on prescribed large batch sizes and whose parameters can be chosen without prior knowledge of the total iteration budget. We show that {\sf RGR-SPIDER} reaches an $\varepsilon$-critical point using $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2})$ iterations and $\mathcal{O}(N+\sqrt{N}\varepsilon^{-2})$ component-gradient evaluations, where $N$ denotes the number of component functions. For the online setting, {\sf RGR-SRM} and {\sf RGR-EMA} achieve iteration complexities of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\varepsilon^{-3})$ and $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\varepsilon^{-4})$, respectively. Experiments on principal component analysis, low-rank matrix completion, and orthogonal convolutional neural networks demonstrate faster empirical convergence than methods that construct recursive gradient estimators directly in Riemannian tangent spaces.

infographic.key_insight: RGR builds recursive gradient estimates in Euclidean space before mapping them to Stiefel tangent spaces, avoiding vector transport while retaining convergence guarantees.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports orthogonality-constrained learning with fewer tuning requirements, including applications to PCA, matrix completion, and orthogonal neural networks.
method: Estimate gradients recursively in Euclidean space, map to tangent space, and update via retraction.
Finite-sum RGR-SPIDER uses an adaptive stepsize requiring neither the gradient Lipschitz constant nor a fixed iteration horizon.
Online RGR-SRM and RGR-EMA require neither prescribed large mini-batches nor a fixed iteration horizon.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports faster empirical convergence on PCA, low-rank matrix completion, and orthogonal convolutional networks, plus an RGR-SPIDER bound of O(N + √N ε⁻²) component-gradient evaluations to reach ε-criticality.
infographic.watch_item: Faster empirical convergence does not necessarily imply lower wall-clock cost; tangent mapping and retraction overhead should be benchmarked.
infographic.paper_title: Recursive Gradient Retraction Methods for Stochastic Nonconvex Optimization on Stiefel Manifolds

title: Functional Subnetwork Localization for Efficient Continual Learning in Large Language Models
authors: Shuoran Jiang, Wentao Zhu, Yang Xiang, Dongfeng Li, Yunan Zhang, Mengchen Zhao
abstract: Biological intelligence continually adapts to new information while retaining prior skills through localized plasticity. In contrast, continual learning in large language models (LLMs) remains vulnerable to catastrophic forgetting. A promising direction is to identify functionally specialized subnetworks within LLMs that enable targeted and resource-efficient adaptation. Using gradient-attribution profiling, we localize cognition-associated functional subnetworks exhibiting extremely low mutual overlap. Building on this finding, we propose Function-isolated Memory-Efficient Optimization (CiMEO), a continual learning framework that routes each training example to its corresponding functional subnetwork, restricting parameter updates and optimizer states to selected regions. Across 1.4 million sequential instructions, CiMEO achieves the highest average performance among the compared methods on five generative benchmarks spanning programming, examination-style tasks, and mathematical reasoning, while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Subspace-overlap and principal-angle analyses further indicate that localized updates help preserve pre-trained representations, highlighting functional subnetwork localization as a practical approach to efficient and stable continual learning in LLMs.

infographic.key_insight: Localizing and selectively updating function-specific LLM subnetworks can reduce catastrophic forgetting while supporting efficient continual learning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: CiMEO restricts parameter updates and optimizer states to selected subnetworks, offering a path to more resource-efficient model adaptation.
method: Identify functional subnetworks using gradient-attribution profiling.
Route each training example to its corresponding subnetwork.
Restrict updates and optimizer states to the selected regions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 1.4 million sequential instructions, CiMEO achieved the highest average performance among compared methods on five generative benchmarks covering programming, examination-style tasks, and mathematical reasoning.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify routing overhead or memory savings, leaving practical efficiency gains to be verified.
infographic.paper_title: Functional Subnetwork Localization for Efficient Continual Learning in Large Language Models

title: Computing Fréchet on Unknown Submanifolds of Riemannian Manifolds
authors: Ian McPherson, Mauro Maggioni
abstract: Empirical averages are fundamental statistical primitives. On nonlinear spaces, their generalization, the Fréchet mean, generally lacks a closed-form solution, and its computation requires solving an optimization problem. We study the computation of intrinsic Fréchet means for data supported on an unknown compact $d$-dimensional Riemannian manifold $M_{1}$ embedded in an ambient metric space $(X,d_{\operatorname{obs}})$. Such settings arise when observations are better represented in non-Euclidean spaces, like probability distributions in Wasserstein space. We assume access only to a local sampler on $M_{1}$ and the observation metric $d_{\operatorname{obs}}$, without knowledge of its intrinsic geometry. We propose a graph-based iterative algorithm that adaptively samples the manifold and approximates geodesic interpolation. Under mild assumptions, we establish an $O(1/T)$ expected objective gap guarantee using at most $\widetilde{O}(T^{4d+3})$ sampled points. As a byproduct of our analysis we extend the metric equivalence guarantees of ISOMAP from Euclidean to Riemannian ambient spaces, which may be of independent interest. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method for computing intrinsic averages on unknown data manifolds.

infographic.key_insight: Intrinsic Fréchet means can be approximated on an unknown manifold using only local samples and an observation metric, without explicit knowledge of its intrinsic geometry.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports intrinsic averaging of non-Euclidean data, including probability distributions represented in Wasserstein space.
method: Adaptively sample the unknown compact manifold and build graph-based approximations of geodesic interpolation.
Iteratively approximate the intrinsic Fréchet mean with an O(1/T) expected objective gap under stated assumptions.
Extend ISOMAP metric-equivalence guarantees from Euclidean to Riemannian ambient spaces.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical experiments demonstrating effectiveness, but gives no datasets, baselines, or quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: The theoretical sample bound, Õ(T^(4d+3)), grows steeply with intrinsic dimension d, raising scalability concerns.
infographic.paper_title: Computing Fréchet on Unknown Submanifolds of Riemannian Manifolds

title: Bias Control and Injection for Multi-Agent Aggregation
authors: Sungjae Lee, Soheil Abbasloo, Jabin Koo, Jungseul Ok
abstract: Multi-agent reasoning with large language models (LLMs) raises a central question for collective decision-making: when agents disagree, whose decision should be trusted? Resolving such disagreements is difficult because agents' decisions are susceptible to non-semantic biases such as majority pressure and response-style preferences, which can obscure the quality of the underlying reasoning. Our analysis shows how bias can be both mitigated and exploited: bias control improves initial answer selection, while bias injection elicits decision instability that serves as a reliability signal. Building on these findings, we introduce a test-time aggregation framework that requires neither validation data nor prior knowledge of relative model strength. The framework implements bias control by presenting one style-normalized reasoning trace per distinct answer, and bias injection by placing each aggregating agent's initially selected answer in the minority. Overall, our framework achieves higher average accuracy and better token efficiency than competing non-oracle aggregation methods across three mathematical reasoning benchmarks and four heterogeneous LLM combinations. It also improves final-answer accuracy when applied to multi-agent debate and Mixture-of-Agents, without modifying their interaction or synthesis processes.

infographic.key_insight: Controlling presentation biases improves answer selection, while deliberately inducing majority pressure exposes decision instability as a reliability signal.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a test-time way to aggregate heterogeneous LLM answers without validation data or prior knowledge of model strengths.
method: Present one style-normalized reasoning trace per distinct answer to reduce style and majority biases.
Place each aggregating agent’s initial choice in the minority to probe decision instability.
Use the resulting reliability signal to guide answer aggregation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three mathematical reasoning benchmarks and four heterogeneous LLM combinations, the framework reports higher average accuracy and better token efficiency than competing non-oracle aggregators, plus accuracy gains for multi-agent debate and Mixture-of-Agents.
infographic.watch_item: Style normalization must preserve reasoning content; the abstract does not establish whether gains generalize beyond mathematical reasoning.
infographic.paper_title: Bias Control and Injection for Multi-Agent Aggregation

title: ParetoChat: An LLM-Based Interface for Interactive Multi-Objective Optimization
authors: Gokhan Ceyhan
abstract: Multi-objective optimization models are often deployed in settings where decision makers (DMs) must balance some conflicting criteria. In practice, however, stakeholders must translate their qualitative preferences between different criteria into numerical weights, priorities, or reference points required by optimization methods, which can be difficult to specify and interpret. This paper proposes \emph{ParetoChat}, an LLM (large language model)-based expert-agent interface for interactive multi-objective optimization. The agent translates natural-language user input into structured scalarization parameters, invokes an optimization system, presents candidate solutions, and iteratively elicits feedback. We describe a multi-agent architecture that separates input processing, multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) expertise, solution presentation, and feedback processing. We then present a simulation study using an LLM-based DM agent and benchmark ParetoChat against interactive methods implemented in DESDEO, including reference-point and NIMBUS methods. The computational experiments on multi-objective binary knapsack and set-partitioning instances show that ParetoChat can guide the search efficiently toward solutions that match the DM's preferences. An application to historical courier-order assignment instances illustrates how users can explore objective extremes and intermediate trade-offs through natural-language requests. The results indicate that LLM agents may provide a practical interaction layer between business stakeholders and optimization tools.

infographic.key_insight: ParetoChat uses LLM agents to translate natural-language preferences into optimization parameters and help users explore trade-offs among conflicting objectives.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It offers an interaction layer that lets stakeholders steer multi-objective optimization without directly specifying numerical weights, priorities, or reference points.
method: Separate agents handle input, decision-making expertise, solution presentation, and feedback.
Translate user preferences into structured scalarization parameters and invoke an optimization system.
Present candidate solutions and refine the search through iterative feedback.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations with an LLM-based decision maker benchmarked ParetoChat against DESDEO reference-point and NIMBUS methods on binary knapsack and set-partitioning problems; historical courier-order assignments illustrated practical use.
infographic.watch_item: Evaluation with a simulated LLM decision maker leaves real-user preference fidelity and interaction reliability to be validated.
infographic.paper_title: ParetoChat: An LLM-Based Interface for Interactive Multi-Objective Optimization

title: When Does Momentum Help in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards?
authors: Kaifei Wang, Zikang Shan, Liwei Wang, Yinyu Ye, Han Zhong
abstract: Momentum is a classical tool for accelerating convex optimization and a standard component of modern large language model training. Yet recent empirical work has questioned the usefulness of first-moment momentum in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). We study this question through a bandit formulation of RLVR with bias-corrected exponential moving average (EMA) momentum, where the EMA coefficient $β$ controls how quickly the weights on past gradients decay. When policy gradients are evaluated exactly, we prove that increasing $β$ within a range that prevents overshoot strictly accelerates optimization. When gradients are estimated from sampled responses, a positive expected gain can be obscured by sampling fluctuations. We show that as the learning rate $η$ decreases, the expected gain with fixed $β$ vanishes faster than these fluctuations, whereas increasing $β$ to keep $η/(1-β)$ within the safe regime preserves a nonvanishing gain that eventually dominates them. Bandit simulations quantitatively validate these predictions. RLVR experiments on Qwen3-4B-Base using SGD with EMA and AdamW support our principle of choosing larger coefficients in practical LLM post-training. On Qwen2.5-32B with AdamW, simply increasing $β_1$ improves mean validation accuracy by nearly $2$ percentage points over the conventional choice, demonstrating the principle's effectiveness at a larger model scale.

infographic.key_insight: Momentum helps RLVR when its coefficient increases as the learning rate decreases, keeping η/(1−β) in a safe regime so expected gains can dominate sampling fluctuations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: RLVR post-training may benefit from tuning momentum jointly with the learning rate rather than retaining a conventional fixed coefficient.
method: Model RLVR as a bandit problem with bias-corrected EMA momentum.
Prove acceleration for exact policy gradients within an overshoot-safe coefficient range.
Analyze sampled-gradient fluctuations and test predictions in bandit simulations and LLM post-training.
infographic.evidence_signal: Bandit simulations validate the predictions, Qwen3-4B-Base experiments support larger momentum coefficients, and increasing AdamW β₁ on Qwen2.5-32B improves mean validation accuracy by nearly 2 percentage points over the conventional choice.
infographic.watch_item: Larger momentum is not unconditionally better: the theory requires an overshoot-safe regime, and its guarantees are derived in a bandit formulation.
infographic.paper_title: When Does Momentum Help in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards?

title: Euler: Towards Human-Centered Multi-Agent Mathematical Discovery
authors: Qiuyu Chen, Qi Wang, Liang Xu, Xin Jin, Baao Xie, Wenjun Zeng
abstract: Mathematical research drives scientific discovery, and recent advances in AI for mathematics have shown that language-model agents can solve challenging problems and develop substantial mathematical proofs. Yet much of today's AI-for-mathematics work centers on obtaining a final answer. This emphasis leaves the exploration behind a result difficult for researchers to understand, while long-running investigations face fragmented context and the risk of unsupported claims propagating across reasoning steps. We present Euler, a human-centered mathematical research system built around a shared, structured representation of the research process. Euler organizes mathematical statements, assumptions, proof dependencies, alternative approaches, failed attempts, and verification evidence into connected research graphs. This representation allows researchers to trace how results are developed and supplies agents with persistent, task-relevant knowledge for planning, collaboration, and verification across sessions. Researchers can also select a graph node linked to a saved team state, revisit the agents' earlier reasoning, and explore alternative directions through continued interaction. We illustrate Euler's capabilities through three mathematical research case studies and describe the implemented system and its software validation.

infographic.key_insight: Euler makes multi-agent mathematical discovery traceable and revisitable through shared research graphs rather than presenting only final answers.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Structured research state can support persistent context, agent coordination, and inspection of proof dependencies across long-running investigations.
method: Connect statements, assumptions, proof dependencies, alternative approaches, failed attempts, and verification evidence in research graphs.
Provide agents with persistent, task-relevant knowledge for planning, collaboration, and verification across sessions.
Let researchers revisit saved team states linked to graph nodes and explore alternative directions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports three mathematical research case studies and software validation, but provides no quantitative performance results.
infographic.watch_item: Recording verification evidence does not itself guarantee proof correctness; the abstract does not specify the strength or coverage of mathematical verification.
infographic.paper_title: Euler: Towards Human-Centered Multi-Agent Mathematical Discovery

title: Gibbs-Gap Policy Optimization for Off-Policy RL with Verifiable Rewards
authors: Xuanchang Zhang, Tong Zhang
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards often trains language models on responses generated by a different, possibly stale behavior policy. Correcting this mismatch with learner-to-behavior importance weights can introduce high variance for long responses. We introduce Gibbs-Gap Policy Optimization (GGPO), which minimizes a log-mean-exp contrast of KL-adjusted rewards among responses to the same prompt, without learner-to-behavior importance weights. We derive GGPO from KL-regularized policy optimization: on policy, its population loss is exactly the KL-regularized optimality gap, and under suitable coverage the learner's single-response expected reward is at least the behavior policy's best-of-$K$ reward, minus terms for the raw finite-group loss, regularization, and finite training data. We characterize reference refresh through exact Gibbs-target composition and a finite-data final-policy reward bound under local reference control and tokenwise behavior mismatch. This refresh is empirically important: in an ablation, fixed-reference GGPO scores $32.96$ on the five-benchmark problem-weighted average, versus $46.58$ with the default refresh schedule. Experiments on mathematical reasoning further show that GGPO outperforms GRPO and AGRO under training-inference mismatch and on fixed offline data, while maintaining its performance as controlled policy staleness grows.

infographic.key_insight: GGPO trains off-policy reasoning models by contrasting KL-adjusted rewards within prompt-level response groups, avoiding high-variance learner-to-behavior importance weights.
infographic.engineering_relevance: GGPO offers a way to reuse stale or fixed response data for verifiable-reward training while remaining robust to policy mismatch in the reported experiments.
method: Minimize a log-mean-exp contrast of KL-adjusted rewards across responses to the same prompt.
Derive the objective from KL-regularized policy optimization, with an exact on-policy population optimality-gap interpretation.
Refresh the reference policy, supported by Gibbs-target composition and conditional finite-data reward bounds.
infographic.evidence_signal: Math-reasoning experiments report gains over GRPO and AGRO under training–inference mismatch and fixed offline data; reference refresh raises the five-benchmark problem-weighted average from 32.96 to 46.58.
infographic.watch_item: Reference refresh is consequential, and theoretical reward guarantees require coverage and mismatch-control assumptions that may not hold for arbitrary offline data.
infographic.paper_title: Gibbs-Gap Policy Optimization for Off-Policy RL with Verifiable Rewards

title: Distributed Performance Boosting through Neural Control for Plug-and-Play Networks
authors: Danilo Saccani, Leonardo Massai, Giancarlo Ferrari-Trecate
abstract: We address the problem of improving the performance of pre-stabilized networked systems subject to plug-and-play (PnP) operations, namely additions or removals of subsystems. While distributed baseline controllers can preserve stability after a PnP transition, augmenting them with expressive neural policies can invalidate the formal stability guarantees. To overcome this issue, we build on recently proposed Performance Boosting controllers based on the Internal Model Control (IMC) principle, which reduce closed-loop stability to a finite $\ell_2$-gain requirement on an auxiliary operator. In the distributed setting, this operator is formed by interconnecting local neural operators that exchange information only between neighboring subsystems. We then derive free parametrizations of this interconnection, namely explicit maps from unconstrained trainable variables to interconnected neural operators satisfying a prescribed network gain bound for every parameter value. The obtained distributed neural controller can therefore be trained by unconstrained gradient-based optimization without stability constraints or projection steps, while retaining the prescribed gain bound at every training iterate. We develop two complementary parametrizations. A neighbor-based compositional parametrization uses local coupling bounds, so that after a PnP event only subsystems whose bounds change need to update their gain parameters. A network-norm parametrization instead uses a bound on the overall coupling matrix and can reduce conservatism, at the price of requiring network-wide information. A PnP DC-microgrid case study shows that the proposed neural layer improves voltage transients under topology changes and load variations while preserving nominal closed-loop stability.

infographic.key_insight: Distributed neural controllers can boost plug-and-play network performance while preserving nominal stability through a guaranteed network gain bound at every training iterate.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables gradient-based tuning of neural control layers for changing networked systems without stability constraints or projection steps.
method: Use Internal Model Control–based Performance Boosting to reduce stability to a finite ℓ₂-gain requirement.
Map unconstrained trainable variables to gain-bounded neural operators that communicate only with neighboring subsystems.
Choose local compositional bounds for targeted updates after topology changes, or a network-norm bound for potentially less conservative design.
infographic.evidence_signal: A plug-and-play DC-microgrid case study reports improved voltage transients under topology changes and load variations while preserving nominal closed-loop stability.
infographic.watch_item: Local bounds may be conservative, while the network-norm alternative requires network-wide information; the stated stability guarantee is nominal.
infographic.paper_title: Distributed Performance Boosting through Neural Control for Plug-and-Play Networks

title: Uncertainty-Aware Budget Allocation for Efficient LLM Tree Search
authors: Jianguo Huang, Zhiyi Lyu, Fuxiang Zhang, Yanchen Deng, Deheng Ye, Bo An
abstract: Tree search enhances multi-step reasoning in large language models (LLMs), yet prevailing methods expand every step with a fixed budget, irrespective of the marginal utility of expansion. We first show, across existing search algorithms, that continuations sampled from a shared intermediate state are largely duplicates and collapse to a few distinct answers. Critically, we find that the semantic dispersion of sibling actions predicts the redundancy of their downstream continuations, permitting a subtree's budget to be fixed before expansion. An information-theoretic analysis motivates this: treating the per-step budget as the Monte Carlo sample size for estimating a step's residual answer entropy, we derive a sufficient budget that shrinks with sibling dispersion. We accordingly propose $\textbf{Uncertainty-Aware Allocation}$ (UAA), a training-free framework that decouples value from uncertainty: values determine which candidates are promising, while uncertainty, estimated from sibling dispersion at no additional model cost, determines how many merit expansion, via uncertainty-aware pruning and uncertainty-aware budgeting. Across mathematical reasoning, logical reasoning, and planning benchmarks, UAA reduces token usage by up to $90\%$ and latency by up to $9\times$ at comparable accuracy, generalizing across four tree search algorithms and both open- and closed-source LLMs.

infographic.key_insight: Semantic dispersion among sibling reasoning actions predicts downstream redundancy, enabling search budgets to be set before expanding subtrees.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Uncertainty-aware allocation can reduce LLM tree-search inference costs while preserving comparable reasoning accuracy.
method: Separate candidate value from uncertainty: value selects promising paths, while uncertainty controls expansion breadth.
Estimate uncertainty from sibling semantic dispersion without additional model calls.
Apply uncertainty-aware pruning and budgeting, motivated by an entropy-estimation analysis.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across mathematical reasoning, logical reasoning, and planning benchmarks, UAA reports up to 90% lower token usage and up to 9× lower latency at comparable accuracy across four search algorithms and open- and closed-source LLMs.
infographic.watch_item: Budgeting depends on sibling dispersion reliably predicting downstream redundancy; the abstract does not establish when this proxy may fail.
infographic.paper_title: Uncertainty-Aware Budget Allocation for Efficient LLM Tree Search

title: When is a better LLM worth paying for? Stochastic Optimization with Switching Mixed-Fidelity Oracles
authors: Swati Gupta, Tianjiao Li
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used upstream of decision-making to clean data, detect label errors, and reconstruct missing values. Yet LLM-assisted data curation creates a new operational tradeoff: higher-fidelity models and richer prompts can be substantially more expensive, while the value of this additional fidelity depends on the downstream optimization accuracy. This raises the central question of this work: when should one pay for a better LLM, given a specific downstream task at hand? We study this question through stochastic optimization with mixed-fidelity first-order oracles, which can have systematic bias and state-dependent variance. We develop two cost-aware algorithmic frameworks that allow adaptive switching between stochastic oracles. With known bias, the first meta-algorithm applies a restarted, cost-aware policy that adaptively selects oracle fidelity across optimization stages. Its cumulative cost is no larger than that of the best fixed oracle in hindsight and can be substantially smaller. With unknown bias, we develop a budgeted certification scheme that uses occasional trusted-gradient evaluations to certify the optimization progress and eliminate unsuccessful oracle sources, and show an explicit tradeoff between certification cost and delayed detection of biased sources. We provide concrete realizations of these meta-algorithms by applying biased stochastic gradient extrapolation (SGE) and recursive regularization under state-dependent noise as subroutines. Synthetic and LLM-completion experiments illustrate the qualitative switching behavior predicted by the theory: the adaptive policy skips several expensive LLM oracles and substantially reduces cumulative cost relative to fixed high-fidelity alternatives while achieving comparable accuracy.

infographic.key_insight: Pay for higher-fidelity LLM outputs when downstream optimization accuracy warrants it; adaptive oracle switching can match or beat the cumulative cost of the best fixed oracle in hindsight under the known-bias framework.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Cost-aware fidelity selection can reduce spending on LLM-assisted data curation while targeting the accuracy needed by downstream optimization.
method: Known bias: use a restarted, cost-aware policy to select oracle fidelity across optimization stages.
Unknown bias: periodically evaluate trusted gradients to certify progress and eliminate unsuccessful oracle sources.
Instantiate the frameworks with biased stochastic gradient extrapolation and recursive regularization under state-dependent noise.
infographic.evidence_signal: Synthetic and LLM-completion experiments show adaptive switching skipping several expensive LLM oracles and substantially reducing cumulative cost versus fixed high-fidelity alternatives at comparable accuracy.
infographic.watch_item: Unknown-bias deployment requires trusted-gradient evaluations, with an explicit tradeoff between certification cost and delayed detection of biased sources.
infographic.paper_title: When is a better LLM worth paying for? Stochastic Optimization with Switching Mixed-Fidelity Oracles

title: Why Shallow Neural Networks Learn Sinusoidal Components First: An Orthogonal Polynomial Dynamics Framework
authors: Yanyang Xiao
abstract: Neural networks often learn low-frequency components before high-frequency ones --- a phenomenon called spectral bias or termed F-principle. Many numerical studies have demonstrated this phenomenon, and theoretical studies have sought to explain it. However, several goals remain insufficiently addressed: (1) explaining spectral bias asymptotically, including its origin and why the preferred components are generally sinusoidal; (2) extending the explanation to general activation functions, such as sigmoid and ReLU; (3) making weak assumptions about the data distribution; (4) avoiding aliasing effects, such as those arising in finite-domain Fourier analysis; and (5) developing a theoretical framework applicable to arbitrary networks. We address these goals theoretically by analyzing the eigenvalue decay and eigenvector shapes of the dynamics matrix H, which arises when we expand the network output as a general Fourier series (GFS) in an orthogonal polynomial basis and express the gradient-descent dynamics of the GFS coefficients as ordinary differential equations. The graded structure of H enables an intuitive explanation of spectral bias, while orthogonal polynomial theory helps us analyze how learning bias depends on the activation function and, potentially, the network architecture.

infographic.key_insight: The paper explains spectral bias through the eigenvalue decay and eigenvector shapes of a graded dynamics matrix, linking learning order to sinusoidal components.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a theoretical lens for understanding how activation choices influence which signal components a neural network learns first.
method: Expand network outputs as a general Fourier series in an orthogonal polynomial basis.
Express gradient-descent coefficient dynamics as ordinary differential equations governed by a matrix H.
Analyze H using its graded structure and orthogonal polynomial theory.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical analysis rather than datasets, benchmarks, or quantitative experimental results.
infographic.watch_item: Applicability to arbitrary architectures remains a goal; the abstract does not establish practical predictive accuracy beyond the shallow-network setting.
infographic.paper_title: Why Shallow Neural Networks Learn Sinusoidal Components First: An Orthogonal Polynomial Dynamics Framework

title: ScoutRoute: Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Routing Using Internal Language Model Signals
authors: Rajdeep Pandhare, Delzaan Bharucha
abstract: Efficient expert routing is a fundamental challenge in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) systems, particularly for heterogeneous collections of independently trained Large Language Mod els (LLMs). Existing routing approaches typically rely on jointly trained gating networks, prompt-based predictors, or computationally expensive multi-model inference, limiting their flexibility and efficiency. This paper presents ScoutRoute, a lightweight post-hoc routing framework that predicts expert competence using internal language model signals extracted from a single forward pass through an inexpensive scout model. Hidden-state representations are used to estimate cross-model competence through lightweight logistic probes, while logit-derived confidence measures are incorporated within a domain-aware routing strategy for efficient expert selec tion without modifying the underlying language models. ScoutRoute isevaluatedon fiveopen-weightlanguagemodels across fourbenchmark datasets covering mathematical reasoning, code generation, commonsense reasoning, and multidis ciplinary knowledge. Experimental results show that ScoutRoute consistently outperforms individual routing signals while requiring only a single scout-model inference. The proposed competence probes also achieve superior calibration compared with conventional confidence measures, demonstrating that internal language model representations provide transferable information for accurate and efficient expert routing across heterogeneous language models

infographic.key_insight: ScoutRoute uses internal signals from one inexpensive language model to predict which expert model is best suited to a task.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports lightweight, post-hoc routing across independently trained language models without modifying the underlying models.
method: Run a single forward pass through an inexpensive scout model.
Apply lightweight logistic probes to hidden states to estimate expert competence.
Combine competence estimates with logit-derived confidence in a domain-aware routing strategy.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five open-weight models and four benchmarks spanning math, code, commonsense, and multidisciplinary knowledge, ScoutRoute reportedly outperformed individual routing signals, while its competence probes showed better calibration than conventional confidence measures.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify routing gains or end-to-end latency savings, leaving deployment benefits uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: ScoutRoute: Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Routing Using Internal Language Model Signals

title: Convergence rate of stochastic gradient descent under Łojasiewicz type condition and polynomially controlled noise
authors: Paweł Węgrzyn
abstract: Stochastic gradient methods are widely used for solving optimization problems in many scientific fields. Recently, their popularity has risen due to the increase in machine learning's prominence. Their convergence is often studied under the convexity assumption, which is too restrictive in modern applications. In this paper, we investigate the almost sure convergence rate and expectation under a Łojasiewicz-type gradient domination condition. This framework includes both bounded and decaying noise, as well as noise with controlled polynomial growth. The obtained results extend existing convergence by allowing a broader class of noise sequences and explicitly capturing the effect of their asymptotic behavior on the convergence rate and applicability.

infographic.key_insight: The paper derives almost-sure and expected convergence rates for stochastic gradient descent under a Łojasiewicz-type condition, explicitly accounting for noise behavior.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results can inform convergence analysis for nonconvex optimization when stochastic gradient noise is bounded, decaying, or subject to controlled polynomial growth.
method: Use a Łojasiewicz-type gradient domination condition instead of convexity.
Analyze bounded, decaying, and polynomially controlled noise.
Relate asymptotic noise behavior to convergence rates.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical convergence results but provides no datasets, numerical benchmarks, or empirical evaluation details.
infographic.watch_item: Applicability requires verifying the gradient domination and noise-control assumptions; the abstract does not specify their precise bounds.
infographic.paper_title: Convergence rate of stochastic gradient descent under Łojasiewicz type condition and polynomially controlled noise

title: The Tilted Sampling Problem: Optimism, Posterior Sampling, and Logarithmic Regret
authors: Mohammad Pedramfar, Siamak Ravanbakhsh
abstract: Many modern learning systems are used not to select a single best action, but to sample diverse high-quality outputs. Examples include entropy-regularized reinforcement learning, RLHF, and reward-guided generative modeling. Motivated by these settings, we study tilted sampling: an online learning problem in which the goal is to sample from the Gibbs distribution induced by an unknown reward function. We define sampling regret as the temperature-normalized cumulative KL divergence between the learner's distribution and the Gibbs target, corresponding to the suboptimality gap in entropy-regularized reward maximization. Our framework generalizes recent sampling-based and KL-regularized formulations in bandits and reinforcement learning. Our main contribution is a general regret framework that captures the different uncertainty structure of tilted sampling and classical regret minimization. While standard regret scales as $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ due to first-order uncertainty, sampling regret is governed by squared confidence widths, yielding logarithmic-in-$T$ regret in standard settings at fixed temperature. We develop sampling analogues of UCB and Thompson sampling (UCS and TS$^2$) and provide unified regret decompositions that explain and extend recent logarithmic guarantees, including the first Bayesian sampling-regret decomposition based on new bounds for posterior-random Gibbs distributions. Our results show that learning to sample from a soft-optimal distribution is statistically distinct from learning to identify a hard optimum.

infographic.key_insight: Learning to sample from an unknown reward-induced Gibbs distribution can achieve logarithmic-in-time sampling regret, unlike the typical square-root scaling of classical regret.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers theoretical guidance for balancing output diversity and reward in entropy-regularized RL, RLHF, and reward-guided generation.
method: Define sampling regret using temperature-normalized cumulative KL divergence to the Gibbs target.
Develop UCS and TS², sampling analogues of UCB and Thompson sampling.
Bound regret through squared confidence widths and posterior-random Gibbs distributions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical regret decompositions and logarithmic guarantees in standard settings at fixed temperature, but no empirical evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: Logarithmic guarantees are stated for fixed temperature in standard settings; they should not be assumed for arbitrary models or temperature schedules.
infographic.paper_title: The Tilted Sampling Problem: Optimism, Posterior Sampling, and Logarithmic Regret

title: Learning Warm Starts for the Simplex Method from Measured Solver Cost
authors: Felix Parker, Danielle A. Ripsman, Emmett Springer, Kimia Ghobadi
abstract: Learned warm starts for the simplex method build starting bases using predictions of which variables will be basic at optimality. Prior work has shown that starting bases predicted by graph neural networks can sharply reduce iteration counts, but the time saved may fall well short of the iterations saved. On 25 classes of linear programs (LPs), we find that a strong supervised basis predictor removes two thirds of the dual simplex's iterations but only a third of its time. Two effects explain the gap: the iterations removed by a good start tend to be cheap, and closeness to an optimal basis does not rank starts by cost. We prove that two starts with equal overlap with an optimal basis and equal pivot counts can differ in linear-algebra work by a factor that grows with the square root of the number of rows. Empirically, across the starts of one LP, the pivot count explains 71% of the variance of log solve time, while the CPU instruction count explains 98.5%. We introduce CostStart, which uses supervised prediction for the basis and trains a small policy on measured instruction counts to choose, per LP, how many predicted columns to use, which algorithm and pricing rule to run, and whether to warm-start at all. On unseen LPs of the training classes, including LPs four times the training size, CostStart roughly halves the solve time relative to the solver's default start and is 1.4 to 2.2 times as fast as two published methods retrained on the same data.

infographic.key_insight: Good simplex warm starts must minimize measured computational cost, not just pivot counts or distance to an optimal basis.
infographic.engineering_relevance: CostStart can accelerate LP solving by adapting the starting basis and solver configuration to each problem, while retaining the option not to warm-start.
method: Predict a starting basis with supervised learning.
Train a small policy on measured CPU instruction counts.
Choose how many predicted columns to use, the simplex algorithm, pricing rule, and whether to warm-start.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 25 LP classes, CostStart roughly halved default-start solve time on unseen instances from training classes, including instances four times the training size, and was 1.4–2.2× as fast as two retrained published methods.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization to entirely new LP classes is not established by the reported evaluation.
infographic.paper_title: Learning Warm Starts for the Simplex Method from Measured Solver Cost

title: Towards Learning-Guided Discovery of Extremal Geometric Constructions: A PatternBoost Study
authors: Deepak Ajwani, Paula Carroll, Rishikesh Gajjala, Ananta Manoranjan, Ryan O'Connor, Rajiv Raman
abstract: Extremal constructions play a central role in the design and analysis of algorithms. Integrality-gap instances expose the limitations of relaxations, while hard configurations reveal structural sources of computational difficulty. Such constructions, however, are still typically discovered through a slow, manual process. This paper investigates how machine learning can accelerate their discovery to support algorithm design and analysis. We build on PatternBoost, a framework alternating local search with generation from a trained transformer, using its Axplorer implementation to investigate three problems: integrality gaps for maximum independent set of rectangles, integrality gaps for stabbing unit squares with axis-parallel lines, and hard instances for recursive guillotine cutting. By exploring candidate representations, local search operations, and surrogate models used to rank candidates before exact verification, we carefully adapt the framework to these combinatorial geometry problems.While naive representations and search strategies fail to find non-trivial instances, our tailored adaptation discovers numerous non-trivial constructions. For stabbing unit squares, the method reaches a gap of $20/13\approx 1.54$, improving on the literature's best known lower bound of $3/2$. Purely automated search converges rapidly and then plateaus, prompting the question of what is required to push the bound higher still. We find that initial instance diversity plays an important role: with modest expert input via a structured staircase construction, the system reaches an improved integrality gap of $14/9\approx 1.555$. These results demonstrate that machine learning and domain expertise can be combined to discover new extremal constructions that advance algorithmic lower bounds.

infographic.key_insight: Learning-guided search discovers new extremal geometric constructions, improving the integrality-gap lower bound for stabbing unit squares beyond 3/2.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Combining machine learning with domain expertise can generate stronger stress tests for optimization relaxations and geometric algorithms.
method: Adapt PatternBoost via Axplorer to alternate local search with transformer-generated candidates.
Tailor representations, search operations, and surrogate ranking before exact verification.
Introduce expert-designed staircase seeds to diversify search and overcome plateaus.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three geometric problems, tailored search found non-trivial constructions; for unit-square stabbing, automated search reached 20/13 ≈ 1.538, while expert-seeded search reached 14/9 ≈ 1.556.
infographic.watch_item: Naive representations failed, and automated search plateaued, indicating sensitivity to problem-specific design and initial-instance diversity.
infographic.paper_title: Towards Learning-Guided Discovery of Extremal Geometric Constructions: A PatternBoost Study

title: MGE-PO: Entropy-Aware Credit Assignment for Mathematical Reasoning
authors: Jihao Huang, Guangjia Chai, Zhirui Chen, Lei Wang, Yao Liu, Liu Qi
abstract: GRPO assigns the same group-relative advantage to equally rewarded responses within a question, leaving their generation uncertainty unused. We introduce MGE-PO, centered on four-quadrant (4Q) advantage shaping that combines verified correctness with rollout generation entropy. Correctness determines the sign of an additional correction, while entropy controls its magnitude: lower-entropy successes receive larger bonuses and higher-entropy failures receive larger penalties. An online entropy-based question curriculum supports this credit rule using cached rollout measurements. At the final checkpoint after eight training epochs on Qwen3-8B-Base, adding 4Q across three policy optimization settings yields absolute gains of 3.23-3.69% in six-benchmark macro avg@32 and 4.24-11.06% in macro pass@32. On Qwen2.5-7B-Base, the complete configuration raises four-benchmark macro avg@32 from 41.5% to 45.4%.

infographic.key_insight: MGE-PO refines correctness-based credit assignment with generation entropy, giving larger bonuses to lower-entropy successes and larger penalties to higher-entropy failures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach uses rollout uncertainty to differentiate equally rewarded responses during reinforcement learning for mathematical reasoning.
method: Apply four-quadrant advantage shaping that combines verified correctness with rollout generation entropy.
Use correctness to set the correction’s sign and entropy to control its magnitude.
Support training with an online entropy-based question curriculum using cached rollout measurements.
infographic.evidence_signal: After eight epochs on Qwen3-8B-Base, adding 4Q across three optimization settings improved six-benchmark macro avg@32 by 3.23–3.69 percentage points and pass@32 by 4.24–11.06 points; the full Qwen2.5-7B-Base configuration raised four-benchmark macro avg@32 from 41.5% to 45.4%.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify entropy-measurement overhead or establish generalization beyond the reported models and mathematical reasoning benchmarks.
infographic.paper_title: MGE-PO: Entropy-Aware Credit Assignment for Mathematical Reasoning
